hints: Notice the word fundamental means the particle has no internal structure and is not made of smaller particles.
Recall which of alpha-particle, neutron and proton are built from protons, neutrons or quarks.
Recall which family the electron belongs to and whether leptons have quark structure.
walkthrough: Identify the test: a fundamental particle cannot be split into smaller constituents, while a composite particle is made of quarks or nucleons.
Check the alpha-particle: it is a helium-4 nucleus of $2$ protons + $2$ neutrons, so it is clearly composite.
Check the proton and neutron: both are hadrons made of three quarks, with proton $uud$ and neutron $udd$, so both are composite.
Check the electron: it is a lepton and in the Standard Model it is not made of quarks and has no internal structure.
Therefore only the electron meets the definition of fundamental. This is option B.

options.A: An alpha-particle is made of two protons and two neutrons, so it has internal structure and is not fundamental.
options.B: An electron is a lepton with no quark structure and no smaller constituents in the Standard Model, so it is fundamental.
options.C: A neutron is a hadron made of three quarks ($udd$), so it is composite and not fundamental.
options.D: A proton is a hadron made of three quarks ($uud$), so it is composite and not fundamental.
